sections.title: Executive investment summary: a fully integrated commodity producer at the top of its own cycle

subsections.title: What the company actually does, in plain terms

blocks.text: National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO) is a Navratna Central Public Sector Enterprise under the Ministry of Mines that mines bauxite, refines it into alumina, smelts alumina into primary aluminium, and burns its own coal to make the electricity that the smelter consumes [F] (SCREENER; AR2026 p.25). It was incorporated on 7 January 1981 and its metal has been registered on the London Metal Exchange since May 1989 [F] (PPT Sep 2026). The physical asset base is the Panchpatmali bauxite mines (68.25 lakh tonnes per annum), the Damanjodi alumina refinery (21 lakh TPA), a 4.60 lakh TPA aluminium smelter at Anugola, a 1,200 MW captive power plant, the Utkal-D&E captive coal blocks (40 lakh TPA), 198 MW of wind capacity and a dedicated bulk shipment facility at Visakhapatnam [F] (AR2026 p.25-26).

**How it makes money: two reportable segments and nothing else.** Chemicals (calcined alumina, alumina hydrate, special grade hydrate, plus bauxite produced for captive use) and Aluminium (ingots, T-ingots, sows, billets, wire rods, rolled products, plus captive power) [F] (AR2026 p.319). In FY26 the Aluminium segment produced Rs 12,924.61 crore of external revenue (72.43% of the total) and Chemicals Rs 4,885.24 crore (27.38%), with Rs 33.20 crore of unallocated wind-power revenue [F] (AR2026 p.77). There is no services line, no order book and no contracted backlog: alumina is sold on monthly spot tenders and short-term LME-linked term contracts, and metal is priced off LME plus a premium revised roughly every six months [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026).

**End markets and geography.** Alumina is overwhelmingly an export business and metal is overwhelmingly a domestic business. In FY26 the company exported 13,08,122 MT of alumina and only 13,238 MT of aluminium, while selling 4,61,081 MT of aluminium and 1,38,010 MT of alumina/hydrate domestically [F] (AR2026 p.44). By value, India accounted for Rs 13,027.69 crore (73.5%) and outside India Rs 4,701.54 crore (26.5%) of FY26 turnover [F] (AR2026 p.321). **The company does not disclose a country-level export split anywhere in the evidence reviewed**; management has said only that 40-50% of alumina exports historically went to the Middle East and that this has fallen because of war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz route [MC] (CALL May 2026). End-use markets are disclosed only at industry level, not at company level: in India, electrical 48%, automotive and transport 15%, construction 13%, consumer durables 7%, machinery 7%, packaging 4-6%, other 6% [F] (AR2026 p.78). That is industry context, not NALCO's own customer mix, which is not disclosed [AI].

**Listing status and what it means for the evidence base.** NALCO is not a recent listing: it has been on the BSE since 1992 and the NSE since 1999 [F] (PPT Sep 2026), and this is the 45th Annual Report [F] (AR2026 p.43). The evidence base is therefore long (our statements data carry ten full years plus TTM) and audited by joint statutory auditors appointed by the C&AG, with a supplementary C&AG audit on top [F] (AR2026 p.190). The constraint is different: the President of India holds 51.28% and has held exactly that through every quarter of the last three years [F] (NUMBERS), so the evidence gap is not history but agency - capital allocation, dividend policy and project selection are visible only through the lens of a controlling shareholder whose objectives are not disclosed in financial terms [AI].

Evidence gap to note up front: this report covers the quarter ended June 2026 (Q1 FY27), but the most recent earnings call transcript available is the April 2026 call on Q4 FY26. No Q1 FY27 conference call transcript was available, and the September 2026 investor presentation contains a 'Highlights of Q1 FY2026-27' section header with no quantitative content in the version available to us. Every Q1 FY27 number in this report therefore comes from our statements data, not from company commentary [F] (PPT Sep 2026; NUMBERS).

blocks.text: **Classifying the drivers.** Structural: #1 (integration), #4 (net cash), #7 (Indian demand deficit). Company-specific: #3 (the 5th Stream), #6 (captive coal ramp), #8 (payout policy). Purely cyclical: #2 (the cost-to-realisation gap, which is a price spread, not a cost advantage that can be banked) and #5 (unhedged LME). **The distinction matters because five of the eight rows would survive a $2,000 LME and three would not** [AI].

subsections.title: Bear thesis: the ten strongest reasons not to own it

items: **1. These are cycle-peak earnings and the record proves how far they travel.** Operating margin was 6% in FY20, 32% in FY22, 16% in FY23, 21% in FY24, 45% in FY25 and 44% in FY26; ROCE ran 2%, 34%, 14%, 17%, 44%, 40% across the same years [F] (NUMBERS). Nothing NALCO controls produced that range - it tracks LME [AI]. Anchoring on 40% ROCE is anchoring on the top of a commodity cycle [AI] (also the standing caution in our earlier research notes, (BOARD)).

**2. The alumina half of the business is in a disclosed, management-acknowledged price collapse.** Average alumina realisation fell from $595 in FY25 to $376 in FY26 and management guided $300-310 for FY27 [MC] (CALL May 2026). The Chemical segment's result fell from Rs 3,245.00 cr to Rs 2,034.16 cr, a 37% decline, in the company's best-ever year [F] (AR2026 p.319). The alumina price index fell from 21.42% of LME cash settlement to 12.04% [F] (AR2026 p.45), and long-term contracts that once fetched 15-17% of LME are now being signed at 11-11.5% [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**3. A capital expenditure supercycle is coming that the current free cash flow does not reflect.** Management guides FY27 capex of ~Rs 2,000 cr, FY28 Rs 4,000-5,000 cr, and a peak of Rs 8,000-10,000 cr in FY29-FY30, for a smelter-plus-power programme of Rs 23,000-30,000 cr completing around December 2030 or early 2031 [MC] (CALL May 2026). FY26 capex was Rs 2,068.16 cr [F] (AR2026 p.48). **The peak year is roughly four to five times the current run-rate, and none of it earns revenue before 2031** [AI].

**4. The C&AG has explicitly said the reported profit is overstated.** The Comptroller and Auditor General's supplementary audit states that provisions are understated by Rs 519.18 crore for restoration and decommissioning of the Utkal D&E coal mines, property plant and equipment by Rs 474.73 crore, and that profit for the year is overstated by Rs 44.45 crore [F] (AR2026 p.190-191). Management disputes it and has referred the question to the ICAI Expert Advisory Committee [F] (AR2026 p.192). **The two positions are not reconciled** [AI].

**5. Board governance was non-compliant for the whole year and the exchanges fined the company every quarter.** The Corporate Governance Report states the Board composition was not in compliance with the Companies Act, SEBI LODR or DPE guidelines throughout FY26 for want of independent directors; BSE and NSE levied fines in each of the four quarters (Rs 7,51,660, Rs 5,42,800, Rs 5,42,800 and Rs 5,31,000 at each exchange) [F] (AR2026 p.150, p.171). All three independent directors' terms ended on 31.03.2026 [F] (AR2026 p.64), and one independent director was appointed only with effect from 14.08.2026 [F] (PPT Sep 2026) - implying a gap of over four months with none [AI].

**6. The controlling shareholder is the Government of India and its objectives are not the share price.** Promoter holding has been 51.28% in every one of the last twelve quarters with zero change [F] (NUMBERS). Rs 1,035.98 cr of the FY26 dividend went to the Government of India [F] (AR2026 p.325). Directors are appointed by Ministry order, not by the board, which is the company's own stated reason for the governance breach [F] (AR2026 p.189). Capital allocation, pricing policy and dividend are all exercised inside that frame [AI].

**7. Single-state, effectively single-site operating risk, with a lease clock running.** Mines, refinery, smelter, power plant and coal blocks are all in Odisha [F] (AR2026 p.94). The Panchpatmali South Block lease runs only to 19.07.2029 and Central & North Block to 16.11.2032 [F] (AR2026 p.46). Management believes a government company gets a 20-year renewal but states plainly that any additional royalty premium "is not known to us till now" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). **Note the two sources disagree on which block expires when - see the discrepancies table in the operations part** [AI].

**8. Working capital is heavy and the headline days figure hides it.** Inventory days were 261 in FY26 (353 in FY25) and the cash conversion cycle 152 days (221 in FY25), against working-capital days of minus 6 [F] (NUMBERS). A minus-6 working-capital-days headline is an artefact of a four-day debtor book and a 114-day payable book, not of a lean business [AI].

**9. Employee costs are about to reverse direction.** The CPSE pay revision is due from 1 January 2027, with management guiding a 10-15% increase in the employee bill [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). The Rs 65 crore of savings booked in FY26 came from superannuating senior staff and replacing them at lower grades [MC] (CALL May 2026) - a one-directional arbitrage that ends when the new pay scales land [AI].

**10. The downstream/value-added story has been formally abandoned.** The Utkarsha Aluminium Dhatu Nigam JV with MIDHANI for a 60,000 TPA high-end alloy plant for defence, aerospace and transportation was found commercially unviable - "even the IRR with the capex investment was coming negative" - and the Ministry of Mines has directed winding up [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.90). What replaces it is a 60,000 t wire rod mill and an annealing furnace [MC] (CALL May 2026). **The defence/aerospace optionality that sits in many aluminium narratives does not exist here** [AI].

**11. Input cost inflation is running against the company right now.** Between FY26 average and Q1/Q2 FY27, management disclosed caustic soda Rs 42,000 to Rs 45,000/t, CP coke Rs 44,000 to Rs 56,000/t, CT pitch Rs 53,000 to Rs 57,000/t, aluminium chloride Rs 1,21,000 to Rs 1,30,000/t and HFO Rs 46,000 to Rs 70,000/t [MC] (CALL May 2026). Management conceded on the same call that "cost of production will increase" [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**12. The bauxite mine that is supposed to feed the new refinery is stuck on a local agitation.** Pottangi (3.5 MTPA, 111 million tonne reserve) has its approach road work "Pending (Local agitation)", with operationalisation planned only in Q3 FY27 and production from Q4 FY27 [F] (PPT Sep 2026; AR2026 p.48).

subsections.title: Key debates: what the market may be getting wrong, in both directions

blocks.caption: Five live debates
columns: The case it is wrong (either way)
rows: Is a 44-47% operating margin structural or cyclical?
Integration plus captive coal has re-rated the margin floor

Against: the same assets produced a 6% margin in FY20 and 16% in FY23 with the same integration [F] (NUMBERS). For: captive coal at 40 lakh MT (FY26) versus 28.2 lakh MT (FY25) and a 99 kg/t caustic specific consumption versus 121 kg/t are genuinely new [F] (PPT Sep 2026); [MC] (CALL Feb 2026)
Two consecutive quarters of sub-$2,600 LME with margin holding above the mid-30s [AI]
Does metal strength really offset alumina weakness?
Management's line: "Overall margin will not go down... it will increase our margins" [MC] (CALL May 2026)

The segment accounts already show the offset is incomplete: Chemical result fell Rs 1,210.84 cr while Aluminium rose Rs 1,518.77 cr in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.319). It worked in FY26 because LME rose. It does not work if both fall [AI]
A quarter in which LME falls and the Chemical segment result does not recover [AI]
Is the Rs 23,000-30,000 cr smelter value-accretive or policy-driven?

For accretive: integration means the marginal tonne carries the same low cash cost [AI]. Against: the company's own cost of equity in our DCF model is 15% [F] (NUMBERS), commissioning is 2030-31, and the previous value-added JV was killed for a negative IRR [MC] (CALL May 2026). **No project IRR, payback or return threshold for the smelter is disclosed anywhere in the evidence reviewed** [AI]
Disclosure of the DPR's IRR when the board approves it - management targeted board approval around August-October 2026 [MC] (CALL May 2026)
Is the Rs 8,408 cr cash pile value or dead money?
It funds the expansion, so it is working capital for growth

It is not netted off in the enterprise value used in our valuation data, which is market cap plus borrowings only [F] (NUMBERS). On one reading the stated EV multiples are conservative; on the other, a PSU cash pile earning bank-deposit interest that generated Rs 521.53 cr of interest income [F] (AR2026 p.233) is capital trapped at a return far below the 15% cost of equity in the model [AI]
Whether the cash is drawn down for capex or keeps compounding in term deposits through FY27-28 [AI]
Is the Middle East export loss temporary?

Management itself says revival of the curtailed Middle East smelters "will take around seven to eight months or maybe one year" and that the Strait of Hormuz route is closed [MC] (CALL May 2026). But the deeper driver is Indonesian refinery supply, which is capacity, not conflict [MC] (CALL Feb 2026)
Alumina spot tenders clearing above $350 for a full quarter [AI]

blocks.text: The market appears to be trading NALCO as an LME proxy with a good balance sheet, and on that framing the current price sits close to the base-case fair value in our DCF model [F] (NUMBERS). Our variant view is that the interesting question is not the LME but the **capital cycle**: the company is simultaneously at the top of its earnings cycle, at the bottom of its capital-intensity cycle, and about to invert both. FY26 free cash flow of Rs 4,413 cr was generated at a capex of Rs 2,025 cr against management's guided peak of Rs 8,000-10,000 cr per year in FY29-FY30 [F] (NUMBERS); [MC] (CALL May 2026). Simultaneously, the pay revision lands from 1 January 2027, alumina is guided down to $300-310 from $376, and the only volume growth available is a 1 MTPA refinery selling into a market the company's own annual report calls structurally surplus [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.75). **The variant perception is therefore that the free cash flow yield investors are extrapolating is the peak output of a business about to spend five years converting cash into a smelter that commissions in 2031** [AI]. Against that, the bull's strongest counter is equally simple: the company has Rs 8,408 cr of cash, no debt and a 40% ROCE, and it can be wrong about the smelter for five years without impairing the equity [AI].

blocks.text: All four existing JVs together are 2.59% of consolidated net assets (Rs 560.12 cr) and minus 0.32% of consolidated profit (a loss of Rs 18.75 cr) in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.327). Three of the four have never commenced operations [F] (AR2026 p.328). The group structure is therefore immaterial to earnings and material only as a statement of strategic intent [AI].

**The operating business is forty years old, not new.** Mines, refinery, smelter and power plant were all commissioned between 1985 and 1987 [F] (AR2026 p.20). The current earnings are produced by assets that are largely depreciated: gross fixed assets of Rs 7,551 cr support Rs 17,843 cr of sales, a fixed-asset turnover of 2.36x, the highest in the ten-year record [F] (NUMBERS). This is the mechanical reason a 44% operating margin is arithmetically available at all [AI].

**The genuinely recent parts are three.** (i) Captive coal, whose mining lease was executed only in 2021 and which reached 40 lakh MT only in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.21, p.47). (ii) Captive caustic soda through GNAL, supplying since August 2022 [F] (AR2026 p.90). (iii) The 5th Stream refinery, in commissioning as of June 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.47). **Everything else in the cost structure is legacy.** The correct reading is that the margin expansion of FY25-FY26 is roughly two parts price and one part these three recent integrations, and only the latter is durable [AI].

**The timeline also shows a diversification record that has not converted.** JVs formed in 2010 (Angul park), 2015 (GNAL), 2019 (Utkarsha), 2019 (KABIL). Of these, one is operating and loss-making, one is being wound up, one has an industrial park with "a few units already operational", and one has spent seven years reaching phase-2 exploration on lithium [F] (AR2026 p.90). Red-mud critical-minerals and gallium extraction projects are at pilot scale and management says commercial results are "another two, three years" away [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). **Any thesis that pays for NALCO's critical-minerals optionality is paying for something with a fifteen-year record of not arriving** [AI].

sections.title: The production chain and where value is captured

items: **Step 1 - Mine.** Panchpatmali bauxite mines (Central, North and South Blocks), capacity 68.25 lakh TPA; FY26 excavation 77.01 lakh t and transportation 77.07 lakh t via a 14.6 km single-flight multi-curve belt conveyor, with a second 7.9 km conveyor being installed for the South Block; 98% blast-free mining [F] (AR2026 p.25; PPT Sep 2026). Royalty is LME-linked, running roughly Rs 400-450 per tonne [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Step 2 - Refine.** Damanjodi alumina refinery, 21 lakh TPA across four streams; FY26 alumina hydrate 23.00 lakh t and calcined alumina 22.75 lakh t [F] (AR2026 p.25, p.43; PPT Sep 2026). Caustic soda is the critical input: ~50% from the GNAL JV under a long-term agreement for up to 1,50,000 DMT per annum, balance from the open market at tender-discovered prices [F] (AR2026 p.46); [MC] (CALL May 2026). A dedicated Steam and Power Plant at Damanjodi runs on an 11.43 lakh MT FSA with MCL plus e-auction coal [F] (AR2026 p.46).

**Step 3 - Split the alumina.** Roughly 9.2 lakh TPA of alumina goes internally to the smelter and 11.8 lakh TPA is exported, per the company's own flow diagram [F] (PPT Sep 2026). The conversion ratio is ~1.93 tonnes of alumina per tonne of aluminium [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Internal transfers are made at cost, not at market [MC] (CALL Feb 2026) - **this is the single most important accounting fact about the segment disclosures** [AI].

**Step 4 - Ship or sell.** Alumina exports move through a dedicated bulk facility at Visakhapatnam, four to five shipments a month of ~30,000 t each, priced on monthly spot tenders with typically one of four shipments on an LME-linked term contract at 11-12% of LME [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL Nov 2025). Storage is constrained: ~75,000 t at Vizag, ~45,000 t at the refinery, ~1 lakh t at the smelter, so "whatever we are producing, we have to sell it" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Feb 2026).

**Step 5 - Smelt.** Anugola smelter, rated 4.60 lakh TPA (960 pots), FY26 cast metal 4,71,701 t; consumes ~810 MW continuously [F] (AR2026 p.43; PPT Sep 2026). Carbon inputs (CP coke, CT pitch) and aluminium fluoride are bought in; a long-term MoU has been signed with Numaligarh Refinery Ltd for CP coke supply [F] (PPT Sep 2026).

**Step 6 - Power.** 1,200 MW captive power plant (10 x 120 MW) at Anugola requiring ~72 lakh MT of coal a year; 47.16 lakh MT under FSA with MCL for units 1-8 plus 40 lakh MT from the Utkal-D&E captive blocks in FY26, with e-auction filling a small residual [F] (AR2026 p.46-47); [MC] (CALL May 2026). Grid purchases are minimal - 90 million units imported in 9M FY26 against 5,773 MU generated [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). 30 MW is sold to the grid [F] (PPT Sep 2026).

**Step 7 - Cast and sell metal.** Cast metal products (ingots, T-ingots, sows, billets, wire rods, rolled products) sold mostly domestically at LME plus a pricing-policy premium that includes import customs duty and inland freight, re-priced every three days against LME movement, with the premium itself reset roughly every six months from export tender discovery [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). Domestic realisation runs ~10% above LME, which management confirms is largely the customs-duty wedge [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

subsections.title: Where value is captured, and why

blocks.text: **Value is captured at the smelter, not at the refinery, and the segment accounts prove it.** In FY26 the Aluminium segment earned Rs 5,564.28 cr of segment result on Rs 12,944.71 cr of gross segment revenue; the Chemical segment earned Rs 2,034.16 cr on Rs 6,694.25 cr [F] (AR2026 p.319). On the MD&A's capital-employed basis, Chemical ROCE was 59.06% and Aluminium 158.33% [F] (AR2026 p.77). **The Aluminium segment carries only Rs 3,523.93 cr of capital employed against Rs 3,467.30 cr for Chemicals, despite earning nearly three times the profit** [F] (AR2026 p.77) - because alumina is transferred in at cost, so the refinery's entire economic contribution to the metal chain shows up in the smelter's numbers [AI].

That transfer-at-cost convention has a second consequence that matters for the bear case: **the Chemical segment's disclosed result is the merchant alumina business only.** When management says the alumina price fall "will not affect the margin as a whole because... it is being compensated through metal price" [MC] (CALL May 2026), they are correct that the internally consumed 9.2 lakh tonnes are indifferent to the alumina price. They are describing a hedge that exists only while the metal price is rising [AI].

**Capital intensity and outsourcing.** NALCO is capital-heavy, not asset-light: gross block plus CWIP of Rs 13,946 cr against Rs 17,843 cr of revenue [F] (NUMBERS), capex at 11.3% of sales in FY26 and an average of ~9.9% over the ten-year record [F] (NUMBERS). Outsourcing is confined to two places: mine development at Pottangi via a 25-year MDO contract [F] (AR2026 p.48), and the internal audit function, which is entirely outsourced to external chartered accountancy and cost accountancy firms [F] (AR2026 p.79) - **eight such firms were appointed with effect from 01.01.2026** [F] (AR2026 p.71). The company also employs 16,722 contract workers against 4,864 employees on roll as at March 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.83), which is a material operating-leverage and industrial-relations fact that the employee-cost line does not show [AI].

blocks.text: **On the evidence, essentially the whole book is commodity.** Alumina is sold on spot tender at an index price and management explicitly says "most of our alumina is going on spot tenders" [MC] (CALL May 2026). Metal is sold at LME plus a formulaic premium reset every three days [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The company's own major-products disclosure divides FY26 revenue into just two buckets - Chemical (hydrate and alumina) Rs 4,809.44 cr and Aluminium Rs 12,889.65 cr - with no further product-level granularity [F] (AR2026 p.320). **There is no disclosed branded, specified or approved-supplier product line** [AI].

The only claims to differentiation are (i) special grade hydrate, which at 15,000-20,000 t is under 1.5% of chemical volume and is not being expanded [MC] (CALL May 2026); (ii) alloy wire rod and rolled products, which management itself labels "value added" but which together run at roughly 30,000 t a year of rolled output against 4.72 lakh t of cast metal [E] from [MC] (CALL May 2026); and (iii) the abandoned Utkarsha high-end defence/aerospace alloy plant [F] (AR2026 p.90). **The honest conclusion is that NALCO's advantage is a cost-curve position, not a product position, and the two behave very differently when prices fall** [AI].

The one genuinely protected price element is regulatory, not commercial: the domestic metal premium of roughly 10% over LME is driven by the import customs duty, which management confirmed when asked directly [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). That is a policy-conferred spread, and policy can remove it [AI].

subsections.title: Why each segment moved - management's explanation and our read

blocks.text: **Chemical [MC]:** management attributes the decline entirely to price. "Our prices has gone down by around $219 compared to last financial year, which has resulted into less revenue of around Rs.2,659 crores... We have sold around 3.4 lakh tons of excess of alumina by increasing our volume... which has given us a additional favourable impact of around Rs.1,714 crores. So net adverse impact of alumina is around Rs.784 crores" [MC] (CALL May 2026). Efficiency (caustic specific consumption from ~121 kg/t to ~99 kg/t) added Rs 100-150 cr [MC] (CALL May 2026; CALL Feb 2026).

**Chemical [AI]:** the revenue story is right but the profit story is worse than the revenue story. External chemical revenue fell 14.3% [E] while the segment result fell 37.3% [F] (AR2026 p.319). That gap is operating leverage running in reverse: the company added 3.4 lakh tonnes of volume at a realisation that had fallen 37% [F] (AR2026 p.79), so it absorbed the full variable cost of the extra tonnes for a shrinking contribution. **Chemical segment assets simultaneously grew Rs 1,330 cr and additions to non-current assets grew Rs 1,208 cr** [F] (AR2026 p.320) - the 5th Stream is being built into the segment earning the falling margin [AI].

**Aluminium [MC]:** "if you compare the quarter 1 of aluminum segment price and quarter 2... there is a jump of INR18,000 in price per ton of aluminum. That is one of the major factors" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). For the full year, realisation rose from Rs 2,39,676 to Rs 2,71,571 per MT [F] (AR2026 p.79).

**Aluminium [AI]:** this is almost entirely price, and price the company does not control. Volume rose only 13,605 tonnes (2.95%) because the smelter is already running above rated capacity [F] (AR2026 p.44, p.43). The FY27 volume plan is 4.73 lakh t against 4.72 lakh t achieved [MC] (CALL May 2026) - i.e. approximately zero. **Every rupee of aluminium segment growth from here until the 2031 smelter is an LME rupee** [AI].

**Order-driven versus organic:** neither segment is order-driven in any meaningful sense. Alumina is sold on repeating monthly spot tenders with a partial term component (management targets "at least 50% should be term and 50% should be spot", but then says "at present, we don't have long term because since the pricing is very low") [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL May 2026). Metal is sold continuously into the domestic market at a formula price. **There is no backlog to execute and no book to run down** [AI].

subsections.title: Is the export mix change strategy or mix?

blocks.text: **It is both, and management is explicit about which part is which.** Export value fell 15% while export alumina volume rose 23% [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.79, p.330) - the value decline is price, not a retreat. Simultaneously the company made a deliberate strategic push into domestic alumina: from 41,204 MT to 1,38,010 MT, a 235% increase, with board-approved policies specifically for sale of alumina to MSMEs and bulk domestic sale [F] (AR2026 p.44, p.13), and management targeting 2.5-3.0 lakh t in FY27 [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**But the domestic push is not a margin story.** Management: "there is a difference - hardly any difference of 1,000, 2,000 because of addition of that export incentive that we added... the price difference is not much that is around Rs.2,000 - Rs.1,500 per ton" [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). On a realisation of roughly Rs 33,800/t [E], that is a 4-6% spread, and the export incentive side of it fell in FY26 (chemical export incentives Rs 95.94 cr to Rs 68.72 cr) [F] (AR2026 p.244). **The domestic push is best read as sales-channel diversification against Middle East route risk, not as margin improvement** [AI].

Disclosed foreign-currency monetary balances at 31.03.2026: USD liabilities Rs 101.84 cr against USD assets Rs 224.30 cr; EURO liabilities Rs 48.05 cr against nil EURO assets; other liabilities Rs 0.83 cr [F] (AR2026 p.322). The disclosed sensitivity to a 10% parallel shift is Rs 12.2 cr on USD and Rs 4.81 cr on EURO [F] (AR2026 p.322) - **immaterial against Rs 7,749 cr of PBT** [E]. Forward contracts on foreign currency were Nil at both year-ends [F] (AR2026 p.321), and there are no derivative contracts [F] (AR2026 p.196).

**The balance-sheet sensitivity badly understates the economic exposure** [AI]. Alumina is priced in dollars per tonne and metal in dollars per tonne on LME; a rupee move re-prices roughly 100% of revenue, not the Rs 224 cr of monetary assets. Management gives the exchange rates used (9M FY26 average Rs 87/USD, Q3 Rs 89/USD) [MC] (CALL Feb 2026) but the company discloses no transaction-exposure sensitivity. **This is a genuine disclosure gap** [AI].

items: **Import duty is a direct earnings input.** The ~10% domestic premium over LME is built from "the import custom duty we add and some inland transportation costs" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). An analyst put the duty at 7% and the Director (Finance) declined to elaborate beyond "that policy guideline is there" [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). **A change in the aluminium import duty would flow straight through the domestic realisation of ~73% of revenue** [AI].

**Carbon border regimes are named as a threat by the company itself.** The MD&A cites EU-CBAM, Korea-ETS, Indonesia-IDX Carbon and India's nascent CCTS, and states the differential carbon tax "is expected to impact the competitiveness of the Indian produced Aluminium & products in overseas market" [F] (AR2026 p.76). No quantification is given and no date is attached [F] (AR2026).

**US tariffs are named but not quantified.** "Tariffs cost (US), Compliance costs (Carbon tax) and Geopolitical energy disruptions elevate costs" [F] (AR2026 p.76). NALCO's metal exports were only 13,238 MT in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.44), so direct US tariff exposure appears de minimis; the exposure is indirect, through global metal flows [AI].

**Middle East conflict and the Strait of Hormuz.** Management, April 2026: "now the route is also closed, whatever route is there, whatever alumina was going, it going through the Strait of Hormuz. So that's why we have to take it to some road route. So it's very difficult to predict now" [MC] (CALL May 2026). Three named smelters - Qatalum in Qatar, EGA and Dubal - cut production by around 50% [MC] (CALL May 2026). **The counter-party for NALCO's new smelter technology agreement, EGA, is one of the curtailed producers** [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS); [MC] (CALL May 2026) - a fact worth watching, though the technology agreement and the alumina offtake are distinct relationships [AI].

**Export obligations exist.** Rs 280.00 cr of export obligation under the Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme at 31.03.2026, up from Rs 130.65 cr [F] (AR2026 p.243) - i.e. the capital-goods imports for the expansion carry a contractual export requirement [AI].

blocks.text: **Single-location manufacturing risk is close to absolute.** Every producing asset - bauxite mines, refinery, smelter, captive power plant and captive coal mines - is in Odisha [F] (AR2026 p.94), and the only export gateway is Visakhapatnam [F] (AR2026 p.26). The only geographically diversified assets are the wind plants in Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu, which contribute Rs 30.14 cr of revenue, and two of which have recognised no revenue since 01.04.2019 [F] (AR2026 p.243, p.245). A single state-level regulatory, environmental, law-and-order or weather event touches essentially 100% of the operating business [AI].

subsections.title: Aggregate utilisation and why it moved

blocks.text: There is no disclosed aggregate utilisation series. What is disclosed is production against nameplate for two years, and on that basis **every major unit ran above or at 100% of rated capacity in FY26** [E]: bauxite 112.9%, refinery 108-110%, smelter 102.5%, captive coal 100%. The company's own framing is that it "reached to the upper limit" and "reached to the peak" [MC] (CALL May 2026).

Why utilisation rose: alumina hydrate output went from 20.755 lakh MT to 23.00 lakh MT (+10.8%) and bauxite from 72.62 lakh MT to 77.07 lakh MT (+6.1%) [F] (AR2026 p.43). Management attributes the gain to techno-economic improvement rather than new equipment - caustic soda specific consumption fell from about 121 kg to 99 kg and then 96 kg per tonne of alumina, and grid power purchases were nearly eliminated [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL Nov 2025). Both are real operating gains, both are one-time step-downs rather than recurring annual improvements, and both are now largely banked [AI].

The structural consequence of running everything at 100%: **there is no volume growth available from the existing asset base.** Metal output is capped at roughly 4.7 lakh t until the 0.5 MTPA smelter commissions around December 2030 or early 2031, and the existing refinery is capped at about 23 lakh t [MC] (CALL May 2026). Every rupee of FY27-FY30 revenue growth must therefore come from the 5th Stream, from price, or from nowhere [AI].

sections.title: Capex forensics: a decade of spending parked in construction

blocks.caption: Capex intensity, FY17-FY26 (Rs cr; ratios computed by us)

blocks.text: Capital commitments not provided for stood at Rs 2,755.39 cr at 31.03.2026 against Rs 2,230.93 cr a year earlier [F] (AR2026 p.308). Note that three different FY26 capex numbers appear in the evidence: Rs 2,068.16 cr standalone and Rs 2,071.78 cr consolidated in the Directors' Report [F] (AR2026 p.48), Rs 2,068 cr in the investor presentation [F] (PPT Sep 2026), Rs 2,025 cr in our statements data [F] (NUMBERS), and Rs 2,038.47 cr of cash actually paid for property, plant, equipment and intangibles in the consolidated cash flow [F] (AR2026 p.273). The spread is about Rs 46 cr and **is not reconciled in any document** [AI].

**The central capex finding: a decade of capital expenditure has produced almost no growth in operating assets.** Cumulative FY17-FY26 capex was roughly Rs 12,032 cr [E]. Over the same decade net fixed assets moved from Rs 7,144 cr to Rs 7,551 cr - up Rs 407 cr - while capital work in progress rose from Rs 566 cr to Rs 6,395 cr, up Rs 5,829 cr, and cumulative depreciation was about Rs 6,348 cr [E] (NUMBERS). In other words the money was spent, the old assets depreciated, and the new assets are still under construction. **Rs 6,395 cr, or 24.1% of total assets, earned nothing in FY26** [E].

items: Revenue grew from Rs 7,543 cr (FY17) to Rs 17,843 cr (FY26), an increase of Rs 10,300 cr, against about Rs 12,032 cr of cumulative capex - roughly Rs 0.86 of incremental revenue per rupee of capex [E] (NUMBERS). **That ratio is close to meaningless here**, because almost none of the revenue increase came from the capex: metal volume went from broadly 4.2-4.6 lakh t to 4.72 lakh t and the refinery from four streams to four streams. The revenue increase is overwhelmingly price and alumina volume from debottlenecking, not new capacity [AI].

The reported fixed-asset turnover of 2.36x in FY26 (2.19x FY25) is computed on net fixed assets excluding CWIP [F] (NUMBERS). Including CWIP, effective asset turnover is 17,843 / (7,551 + 6,395) = **1.28x** [E]. The improving turnover trend is therefore partly an artefact of leaving new assets out of the denominator [AI].

Capex of Rs 5,677.4 cr on the 5th Stream (projected) buys 10.0 lakh TPA of alumina capacity. At management's own stated margin of about Rs 11,000 per tonne at full ramp, that is roughly Rs 1,100 cr of annual contribution at 100% utilisation - a five-year simple payback before depreciation, tax and any further alumina price decline [E] (AR2026 p.46; CALL Nov 2025). At the guided FY27 alumina price of $300-310 the margin would be materially thinner, and management declined to restate the project IRR when asked directly: "It is very difficult to calculate the IRR" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

subsections.title: Pass-through: the claim and the evidence

blocks.text: Management's claim is that cost inflation is absorbed by efficiency and by metal prices: "whatever extra cost we are incurring in the input cost, that will be set up by our fixed cost" and "Alumina might be down. But for NALCO overall, I think there will be no impact on the price front" [MC] (CALL May 2026). Asked directly whether cost of production would rise, the CMD answered "Yes, yes cost of production will increase" [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**There is no pass-through mechanism.** Metal is priced off LME plus a premium that management revises roughly every six months through an export tender and explicitly does not link to input costs [MC] (CALL May 2026). Alumina is sold on monthly spot tenders. The company does not hedge anything - "Hedging, we are not doing" - and the annual report confirms nil commodity derivatives against Rs 12,889.65 cr of aluminium exposure [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.170). So margin is the arithmetic difference between two independent price series, one of which the company cannot influence and neither of which it hedges. Management's "compensation" argument is a statement about historical correlation between LME and alumina, not a contractual pass-through - and in FY26 that correlation broke down, with metal up 26% and alumina down 37% simultaneously [F] (AR2026 p.79) [AI].

A $100 per tonne move in the LME on 4.74 lakh tonnes of metal is worth roughly Rs 412 cr at the FY26 exchange rate of about Rs 87/$ [E], and a $10 per tonne move in alumina on 14.46 lakh tonnes is worth about Rs 126 cr [E]. **So roughly a 20% shock to every purchased input equals a $200 LME move - and the LME moved from $2,526 to $2,772 in FY26 and to about $3,600 in Q1 FY27** [F] (AR2026 p.45); [MC] (CALL May 2026). Input costs are a second-order driver of this P&L; price is first-order by a wide margin [AI].

Read that both ways. It means input inflation, however alarming the individual line items look, cannot break the thesis on its own. It also means no amount of procurement discipline, captive coal or caustic soda efficiency can protect earnings if the LME halves - which it has done before within this ten-year record [AI].

The company is not required to disclose these and does not [F] (AR2026, whole document reviewed).

But applying them to disclosed volumes reproduces the audited segment results to within a few percent in both segments [E]. That is meaningful independent corroboration that the Rs 1,55,000-1,60,000 per tonne metal cost and Rs 20,000-22,000 per tonne alumina cost are approximately right - and therefore that the metal business is earning roughly 41% of realisation as contribution while alumina earns roughly 38% [E].

subsections.title: The internal transfer and the alumina balance

blocks.text: Alumina is transferred to the smelter at cost, not at market: "We are transferring the alumina to our smelter plant on cost" [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The Chemical segment's intersegment revenue was Rs 1,809.01 cr in FY26 against Rs 1,910.01 cr in FY25 [F] (AR2026 p.254). At a stated ratio of 1.93 tonnes of alumina per tonne of aluminium [MC] (CALL Feb 2026), the 4.717 lakh t of cast metal implies about 9.10 lakh t of internal alumina consumption [E], which matches the presentation's stated "Alumina Internal Consumption 9.2 lakh TPA" [F] (PPT Sep 2026).

**The transfer convention systematically flatters the Aluminium segment and penalises Chemicals.** Because 9.1-9.2 lakh t of alumina - about 39% of refinery output - moves to the smelter at cost rather than at the $376/t market price, the Chemical segment reports zero margin on its largest single customer while the Aluminium segment reports a 43.17% PBIT margin and a 158.33% return on capital employed [F] (AR2026 p.77). **Neither segment number should be read as an economic return.** The Aluminium segment's 158% ROCE is an accounting artefact of a fully depreciated smelter being fed free-of-margin alumina [AI].

subsections.title: What would have to be true for unit economics to improve

items: **Alumina price recovery.** The alumina price index fell from 21.42% of LME cash settlement in FY25 to 12.04% in FY26, and long-term contracts that once fetched 15-17% of LME are being signed at 11-11.5% [F] (AR2026 p.45); [MC] (CALL May 2026). Recovery requires Indonesian refinery supply to be absorbed by new Indonesian and Thai smelting capacity, which management expects "maybe next year" [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). **Outside the company's control** [AI].

**The 5th Stream running at its designed efficiency.** Management expects lower manpower per tonne and lower caustic consumption from high-pressure/medium-pressure digestion, offset by depreciation, netting to cost "almost same or maybe one or two thousand more" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). **On management's own numbers the new stream is per-tonne worse, not better** [AI].

**Pottangi bauxite at unchanged royalty.** Quality is stated at about 42% alumina content and royalty is LME-linked at roughly Rs 400-450 per tonne, with management saying "On the new mines also the royalty will be same" [MC] (CALL May 2026). If the 2029 South Block renewal carries an iron-ore-style 150% premium, bauxite cost rises across the whole chain [AI].

**Captive coal at 48 lakh MT.** The gap between captive and linkage coal is now only Rs 200-300 per tonne after the GST compensation cess was removed from linkage coal [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). **The remaining captive-coal benefit is therefore small** - roughly Rs 24 cr on an 8 lakh MT increment at Rs 300/t [E]. The bigger prize already captured was eliminating grid power purchases, worth about Rs 136 cr in H1 FY26 alone [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

**Value-added mix.** Rolled products at ~2,000 t per month and a planned 60,000 t wire rod mill together amount to a low-single-digit percentage of 4.7 lakh t of metal [MC] (CALL May 2026). The ingot-to-wire-rod premium actually *fell*, from about $10,000 to $6,000-7,000 per the November-quarter commentary, so mix improvement is not currently paying [MC] (CALL Feb 2026) [AI].

**Scrap-fed casting.** Casting capacity exceeds hot metal capacity by 50,000-1,00,000 t, and management is trying to buy good-quality scrap to fill it but "now we are not able to get good quality scrap" [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). This is the only genuinely incremental volume lever available before FY31, and it is stalled on sourcing [AI].

sections.title: Reading the statements like a forensic analyst

blocks.text: Our statements data are **consolidated** and cover ten full years plus a trailing twelve months, with twelve quarters of quarterly data and a latest quarter of June 2026 [F] (NUMBERS). The annual report's Management Discussion and Analysis and Directors' Report tables are **standalone** [F] (AR2026 p.79-83). Almost every apparent disagreement between the company's headline numbers and ours is this basis difference, and we reconcile it below rather than leaving it hanging. Two genuine limitations remain: our data source does not split cash out of the "other assets" line, so the Rs 8,407.74 cr of cash and bank is invisible in the summarised balance sheet [F] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.81); and no prior-quarter coverage file exists, so this is initial coverage with no like-for-like predecessor to test.

items: **Growth is margin, not volume.** Sales CAGR was 10.0% over nine years, 14.8% over five and 7.8% over three; EBITDA CAGR was 24.8%, 34.8% and 50.2% over the same windows [F] (NUMBERS). A three-year EBITDA CAGR of 50% on a three-year sales CAGR of 8% is a price story, not an operating story [AI].

**FY26 is the cleanest illustration in the record.** Alumina volume rose 31% and metal 3%, yet Chemical segment revenue *fell* 12% from Rs 7,607.44 cr to Rs 6,694.25 cr and total revenue rose only 6.3% [F] (AR2026 p.254, p.79). Management quantified it: Rs 2,659 cr of adverse price offset by Rs 1,714 cr of favourable volume, a net Rs 784 cr adverse in alumina alone [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Other income is the cash pile's yield and it is about to be spent.** Other income was Rs 665.83 cr in FY26 (of which interest income Rs 579.95 cr), 8.6% of PBT, against 5.0% in FY25 and 25.0% in FY24 [F] (AR2026 p.79, p.273); [F] (NUMBERS). It rose 86.5% because the investible surplus grew [F] (AR2026 p.79). **As the Rs 8,408 cr cash balance is consumed by the smelter programme, this line reverses** [AI].

**Finance cost rose with no debt.** Interest went from Rs 59 cr to Rs 100 cr while borrowings fell to nil, because "the interest component of the settlement will be put under finance cost" - a litigation settlement, concentrated in the December 2025 quarter where quarterly interest jumped to Rs 60 cr from Rs 8 cr [F] (AR2026 p.80); [MC] (CALL Feb 2026); [F] (NUMBERS). The settlement itself is not quantified in any document [AI].

**Depreciation is about to step up.** FY26 depreciation was Rs 745.36 cr against a CWIP balance of Rs 6,395 cr that management expects to capitalise substantially in FY27: "I think 100% will be capitalized this year because the majority is towards the fifth stream expansion. It is around Rs.5,500 crores" [F] (NUMBERS); [MC] (CALL May 2026). **A Rs 5,500 cr capitalisation at, say, a 25-year life adds roughly Rs 220 cr of annual depreciation** [E] - and the annual report already notes higher FY26 depreciation "due to capitalization of assets" [F] (AR2026 p.81).

**Two unexplained items in the record.** The FY21 effective tax rate was 1% against 22-39% in every other year [F] (NUMBERS) and no document in the evidence explains it. Quarterly depreciation was Rs 88 cr in March 2025 against Rs 286 cr in the immediately preceding quarter and Rs 211 cr in March 2026 [F] (NUMBERS) - a sequence that implies a year-end true-up, again unexplained [AI].

**Provisioning is lumpy and discretionary at the margin.** FY26 Q4 carried about Rs 40 cr for red mud pond closure and about Rs 54 cr for fly-ash transportation, both non-cash [MC] (CALL May 2026); Q3 FY26 carried a roughly Rs 50 cr write-back of an excess performance-related-pay provision [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The segment note shows "material non-cash expenditure" of **negative Rs 72.59 cr in FY26 against positive Rs 67.46 cr in FY25** - a Rs 140 cr swing in the direction of releasing provisions [F] (AR2026 p.254). That is not a large number against Rs 7,749 cr of PBT, but the direction is worth watching [AI].

**Net cash, at scale, and it does not appear where a reader would look for it.** Cash and bank was Rs 8,407.74 cr at 31.03.2026 against Rs 5,426.73 cr a year earlier - a 55% increase - and consists of bank deposits classified as short-term investments [F] (AR2026 p.81). In the summarised statements this sits inside "other assets" of Rs 12,065 cr, which is why that line looks alarmingly large [F] (NUMBERS). **Roughly 70% of the "other assets" line is money in the bank** [E].

**Twenty-four percent of the asset base earns nothing.** CWIP Rs 6,395 cr on total assets of Rs 26,544 cr [F] (NUMBERS). Net fixed assets have been effectively flat for a decade at Rs 7,144-7,651 cr [F] (NUMBERS).

**Intangibles are mining rights, not goodwill.** Of Rs 897.92 cr, Rs 845.66 cr is mining rights - net present value paid for forest land, compensatory afforestation and wildlife management for Panchpatmali, Pottangi and the Anugola coal mines - with Rs 634.73 cr added in FY25 [F] (AR2026 p.226). There is no goodwill on the balance sheet because there are no acquisitions and no subsidiaries [F] (AR2026 p.171).

**No debt, and the Rs 60 cr that looks like debt is not.** Our data show FY26 borrowings of Rs 60 cr and FY25 of Rs 182 cr; the annual report shows borrowings of nil and Rs 124.22 cr with lease liabilities of Rs 59.83 cr and Rs 57.52 cr. The two reconcile exactly: our source adds lease liabilities to borrowings [E] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.82). The FY25 borrowing itself was a letter-of-credit facility availed with recourse; in FY26 the company accepted LCs without recourse so nothing is recognised [F] (AR2026 p.82).

**Contingent liabilities are Rs 2,179.22 cr, up from Rs 2,050.43 cr**, or 10.1% of net worth [E] (AR2026 p.307). The largest single item is a Rs 901.45 cr claim from public sector undertakings - principally Odisha Hydro Power Corporation's energy compensation and delayed payment surcharge claim dating from 2005 - which rose Rs 201.04 cr during FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.307-308). GST contingents rose from Rs 37.55 cr to Rs 161.57 cr [F] (AR2026 p.308).
**Commitments are Rs 2,755.39 cr** of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account [F] (AR2026 p.308).

**Off-balance-sheet exposure to the caustic soda JV.** A Rs 200 cr financial guarantee to joint ventures remains outstanding [F] (AR2026 p.199), and the company has given backstopping support on GNAL's Rs 500 cr compulsorily convertible debentures in proportion to its 40% holding, with mandatory and accelerated put options granted to the investor; Rs 147.36 cr of "deemed investment" is recognised, comprising Rs 124.15 cr of financial liability and Rs 23.21 cr of unremunerated financial guarantee [F] (AR2026 p.227-228).

**Equity reconciles cleanly between bases.** Standalone net worth is Rs 21,862.76 cr and consolidated Rs 21,603 cr; the Rs 259.8 cr difference is cumulative equity-accounted joint venture losses [E] (AR2026 p.94; NUMBERS).

**Cash conversion is good and has been good for a decade**, with two exceptions. CFO/PAT was 1.11x in FY26, 1.10x in FY25, 1.15x over three years and 1.14x over five [F] (NUMBERS). The exceptions are FY20 (CFO minus Rs 349 cr on PAT of Rs 136 cr, a ratio of -2.57x) and FY23 (0.63x) - **both cycle troughs, which is precisely when a commodity producer's cash flow inverts** [F] (NUMBERS) [AI].

**FY26 CFO of Rs 6,438 cr included a Rs 361.93 cr working capital release** [E], built from inventories +Rs 71.03 cr, other assets +Rs 247.85 cr, trade payables +Rs 67.21 cr, provisions +Rs 33.89 cr against receivables -Rs 28.29 cr, other financial liabilities -Rs 20.06 cr and other liabilities -Rs 23.29 cr [F] (AR2026 p.273). About 5.6% of CFO is therefore a one-off release, not operating generation [E].
**Tax paid tracks tax charged.** Rs 1,921.53 cr paid against Rs 1,951.69 cr expensed [F] (AR2026 p.273) - no evidence of aggressive deferral.

**The investing outflow is mostly not investment.** Of Rs 4,199.92 cr of investing outflow, Rs 2,851 cr was a net movement into bank term deposits and only Rs 2,038.47 cr was actual capital expenditure on property, plant, equipment and intangibles [F] (AR2026 p.273). Read literally, our data's CFI of -Rs 4,200 cr overstates capital intensity by roughly 40% [E].

**Financing is dividends and almost nothing else.** Rs 2,206.00 cr of outflow, of which Rs 2,020.30 cr was dividends paid, Rs 124.22 cr repayment of the LC facility, Rs 56.86 cr finance cost and Rs 4.62 cr lease payments [F] (AR2026 p.273).

**Cumulative free cash flow was Rs 10,129 cr over three years and Rs 12,197 cr over five** [F] (NUMBERS) - which is why the balance sheet carries Rs 8.4k cr of cash despite a 36% dividend payout. **That reservoir is the funding plan for the smelter** [AI].

subsections.title: The headline, and why it misleads

blocks.text: Working capital days were **minus 6** in FY26 and minus 7 in FY25, which would ordinarily describe a business funded by its suppliers [F] (NUMBERS). The same data set reports a **cash conversion cycle of 152 days** in FY26 and 221 days in FY25 [F] (NUMBERS). Both are correct and they measure different things: working capital days net all current assets against all current liabilities, including a Rs 8,408 cr cash pile that swamps everything else, while the cash conversion cycle is built from inventory, debtor and payable days computed on a materials-cost base [AI]. **A reader who quotes minus 6 days has said nothing about how this business consumes cash** [AI].

blocks.text: **The 261-day inventory figure is not nine months of stock.** On a revenue base, inventories of Rs 1,834.90 cr against revenue of Rs 17,843.05 cr are 37.5 days [E]. The 261-day figure arises because the ratio is struck against purchased materials cost rather than sales, and NALCO buys very little of what it sells - it mines it. **For a vertically integrated miner, materials-based inventory days are a structurally misleading metric and should be discarded** [AI]. The same caution applies to the 152-day cash conversion cycle, which inherits the distortion.

items: **Finished goods were run down to support the volume record.** Finished goods fell 31% from Rs 650.64 cr to Rs 449.87 cr while raw materials rose 66% to Rs 179.52 cr and carbon anodes rose 27% to Rs 230.54 cr [F] (AR2026 p.298). Management corroborated the destocking: alumina stock at the smelter fell from about 15 days to 10-12 days [MC] (CALL Feb 2026).

**Storage is physically capped, so production is forced into the market.** "We cannot store a lot of material there. So, whatever we are producing, we have to sell it" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). Against 14.46 lakh t of annual alumina sales the company holds roughly 2.2 lakh t of total alumina storage across Vizag, the refinery and the smelter [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). **This is a structural price-taking weakness disguised as working capital efficiency: NALCO cannot withhold tonnage to defend price** [AI].

**Payable days are falling for policy reasons, not commercial ones.** From 206 days (FY24) to 137 (FY25) to 114 (FY26) [F] (NUMBERS), while the company is registered on all five RBI-approved TReDS platforms, procured Rs 1,447.94 cr from micro and small enterprises (61.56% of eligible procurement against a 25% mandate) and routed Rs 4,200 cr of procurement through GeM [F] (AR2026 p.90-91; PPT Sep 2026). **Faster supplier payment is a government objective being met with shareholder working capital** - defensible policy, real cash cost [AI].

**Receivables are essentially an export letter-of-credit book.** Four days of debtor days on Rs 4,701.54 cr of export turnover implies near-immediate settlement [F] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.79). The 15% increase in receivables is explained as credit sales against letters of credit pending realisation at the reporting date [F] (AR2026 p.82).

subsections.title: The C&AG disagreement, and what it means

blocks.text: The Comptroller and Auditor General states that non-current provisions of Rs 307.51 cr **exclude Rs 519.18 cr** of liability for restoration, rehabilitation and decommissioning of the Utkal D&E coal mines under the approved Mine Closure Plan, which understates provisions by Rs 519.18 cr and property, plant and equipment by Rs 474.73 cr, understates expenses by Rs 32.88 cr and depreciation by Rs 11.57 cr, and **overstates profit for the year by Rs 44.45 cr**. The C&AG adds that the escrow balance needs to be reviewed to match the mine closure obligation [F] (AR2026 p.190-191).

Management's reply is that provision is being made per the Ministry of Coal office memorandum of 25.01.2025 at Rs 14,00,000 per hectare for the full 862.53 hectares, escalated and discounted under Ind AS 37, with escrow deposits strictly per the guidelines and a final mine closure plan due five years before closure, so "there is no short provisioning". It has referred the question to the ICAI Expert Advisory Committee [F] (AR2026 p.192).

**Three observations a buy-side reader should not skip.** First, the amount at stake in the P&L is small - Rs 44.45 cr against Rs 5,797 cr of PAT, 0.8% [E] - so this is not an earnings-quality crisis. Second, the balance-sheet amount is not small: Rs 519.18 cr of unrecognised obligation against a Rs 21,603 cr net worth, and it will grow as the mine expands from 40 to 48 lakh MT [E]. Third, and most important, **the two audit layers disagree**: the statutory auditors, who see the working papers, issued an unmodified opinion and did not treat the item as a modification, while the C&AG, who by its own account worked "without access to the working papers of the statutory auditor", says profit is overstated [F] (AR2026 p.190, p.193). Neither document explains the divergence, and the company has escalated it to a third party. **We treat this as unresolved and record both positions** [AI].

items: **No fraud.** "No fraud by the Company or any fraud on the Company has been noticed or reported during the year"; no ADT-4 filed; no cases reported under section 143(12) [F] (AR2026 p.200; p.187 area of the Directors' Report).
**No restatement** is disclosed anywhere in the evidence; prior-year figures are described only as "regrouped wherever necessary for uniformity in presentation" [F] (AR2026 p.273).

**No common-control or unusual accounting.** There are no subsidiaries at all, so no consolidation judgement beyond equity-accounting four joint ventures; no business combinations; no goodwill [F] (AR2026 p.171, p.200).
**Cost records** are maintained under section 148(1) and the auditors report them prima facie in order, without detailed examination [F] (AR2026 p.199).

**Internal financial controls**: a separate unmodified report; internal audit is outsourced to external chartered accountant and cost accountant firms across all locations; no reportable material weakness was observed [F] (AR2026 p.196, p.201, p.79).
**Physical verification**: PP&E on a rolling three-year programme with immaterial discrepancies; inventories verified with no discrepancy of 10% or more in any class [F] (AR2026 p.198-199).
**Statutory dues** generally deposited on time, with nothing undisputed outstanding beyond six months [F] (AR2026 p.199).

**A regulatory compounding**: Rs 10,00,000 approved by the Indian Bureau of Mines towards settlement of a violation of Regulations 13(1) and 45(7) of the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules for **excavation beyond the permitted limit**, paid on 24.01.2026 [F] (AR2026 p.171). Small in rupees; notable in kind, given that FY26's headline achievement was bauxite output 12.9% above nameplate [AI].
**Managerial remuneration limits do not apply** - section 197 and Schedule V are disapplied for government companies by MCA notification G.S.R. 463(E) of 05.06.2015 [F] (AR2026 p.196).

blocks.text: **What the documents do not cover**, and a reader should not assume: the contents of the C&AG's own audit report on the company (only the section 143(6)(b) comments are reproduced); the cost audit report; the details or outcome of the one whistle-blower complaint; the carrying value of the two idle Rajasthan wind plants; the quantum of sanctioned bank working capital limits; any quantification of the ORISED exposure; the amount of the litigation settlement that produced FY26's finance cost increase; and the internal audit findings. None of these is a required disclosure; all of them are gaps in what can be verified [AI].

**Overall accounting-quality assessment: solid mechanics, contested judgement.** The ledger ties out, cash conversion is real, tax paid matches tax charged, there is no fraud, no restatement and no related-party leakage. But three judgement areas are open: an unquantified twenty-one-year tax exposure on the core mineral asset, a Rs 519.18 cr provision the state auditor says is missing, and seven years of idle wind assets carried at undisclosed value. On a ten-point scale we would place accounting quality at 4 - not because of what is wrong, but because of how much is unquantified where quantification is possible [AI].

blocks.text: **The governance record for FY26 is a documented, continuous statutory breach.** The Corporate Governance Report states plainly that board composition "was not in compliance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 and DPE Guidelines on Corporate Governance due to absence of requisite number of Independent Directors", that Regulation 17(1)(a) was breached for specified periods and 17(1)(b) "throughout the year" [F] (AR2026 p.150-151). The secretarial auditor quantified the gap: with an executive chairman the company needed **eight** independent directors and had **three** [F] (AR2026 p.189). Fines were levied by both exchanges in every quarter of FY26 - Rs 7,51,660, Rs 5,42,800, Rs 5,42,800 and Rs 5,31,000 at BSE and the same at NSE - following two quarters of fines in FY25 and none in FY24 [F] (AR2026 p.171). Then all three independent directors left on 31.03.2026 and the next appointment took effect on 14.08.2026, implying roughly four and a half months with effectively none [F] (AR2026 p.150; PPT Sep 2026) [AI].

In fairness, the company's explanation is structural and correct: "NALCO being a Government Company, the power to appoint Directors, including Independent Directors, rests solely with the Government of India" [F] (AR2026 p.189). The Board instructed the CMD to press the Ministry, the matter was escalated repeatedly, and waivers have been sought from both exchanges [F] (AR2026 p.171). **The breach is not a management choice. But it is not a cost-free technicality either**: the Audit Committee and Nomination & Remuneration Committee could not be reconstituted even after the August 2026 appointment [F] (PPT Sep 2026), which is precisely the governance machinery a minority shareholder relies on while a Rs 23,000-24,000 cr capital programme is approved [AI].

subsections.title: Alignment and skin in the game

items: **Promoter holding: 51.28% in every one of the last twelve quarters, with a one-year change of exactly zero** [F] (NUMBERS). The holder is the President of India / Government of India [F] (AR2026 p.323; PPT Sep 2026). There has been no buying, no selling and no creeping acquisition.

**No pledges are disclosed anywhere in the evidence.** Our earlier research notes record explicitly that third-party pledging and insider-activity endpoints were unreachable during that run and are therefore **UNCHECKED**, not verified clean [F] (BOARD). We carry that caveat forward rather than asserting an absence [AI].

**Directors own no shares.** The AGM annexure states for each of the three directors seeking appointment or re-appointment that they hold no share in the company [F] (AR2026 p.12-13). Independent directors are not entitled to stock options [F] (AR2026 p.150). There is no ESOP scheme in the evidence.

**There is therefore no equity alignment at all between management and shareholders.** Remuneration is salary and DPE-scale benefits; the entire upside from a Rs 23,000-24,000 cr capital decision accrues to shareholders and none of it to the decision-makers, which cuts both ways - no incentive to inflate the share price, and no financial consequence for destroying capital [AI].

**Compensation is trivially small relative to the business.** Total KMP remuneration was Rs 7.52 cr in FY26 across eight whole-time directors (some part-year) plus the Company Secretary, against Rs 5,797 cr of PAT - 0.13% [E] (AR2026 p.325). Section 197 and Schedule V managerial remuneration limits do not apply to government companies [F] (AR2026 p.196).

**Self-dealing indicators: none found.** No non-cash transactions with directors (CARO xv), loans to KMP nil at year-end with a maximum of Rs 0.02 cr during the year, related-party transactions compliant with sections 177 and 188, one whistle-blower complaint received per the Corporate Governance Report and none per the CARO annexure (unreconciled) [F] (AR2026 p.201, p.325, p.171).

**Institutional ownership has rotated hard.** Foreign institutions went from 8.99% (Mar 2024) to 22.27% (Mar 2026) and 21.99% (Jun 2026), while domestic institutions went from 18.82% to 10.75% and 11.22% [F] (NUMBERS). **Foreign money bought roughly the whole of what domestic institutions sold through the re-rating** - a divergence of view between two professional investor bases that a reader should treat as information [AI]. The public float fell from 20.93% to 15.52% and shareholder count stands at about 9.49 lakh [F] (NUMBERS).

blocks.text: **The inference is stark: roughly 89% of Indian primary aluminium production comes from producers that NALCO never names in any document** [E]. NALCO is also a marginal metal exporter - 13,238 tonnes against an Indian primary-producer export total of 1.648 Mn MT - while being a very large alumina exporter [F] (AR2026 p.44, p.78). The company's competitive identity is therefore inverted from how it is often described: **it is a domestic metal seller and a global alumina seller, not a global metal player** [AI].

subsections.title: Competitors named by management, and what they really are

items: **No domestic competitor is named on any of the three calls.** Not one question or answer identifies an Indian rival by name [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026).

The entities management does name are **price-setters, not customer competitors**: Indonesian refineries (two or three new units creating alumina surplus), Middle East smelters **Qatalum (Qatar), EGA and Dubal** which cut output by about 50% on war disruption, an Icelandic smelter closure, Chinese production capped at 45 Mn TPA against 46 Mn TPA of consumption need, and Thai smelting capacity capped at 45 against 60-plus [MC] (CALL May 2026; CALL Feb 2026). These determine the alumina and LME prices NALCO receives; they do not bid for NALCO's Indian metal customers [AI].

**The irony is worth recording**: EGA, cited on the May 2026 call as a Middle East smelter whose curtailment was distorting alumina demand, signed a technology partnership with NALCO for the 0.5 MTPA brownfield smelter on 7 September 2026 [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS). A price-affecting counterparty has become a technology supplier.

The annual report's competitive discussion is at industry level and describes threats from **imports of value-added products, pressure on domestic downstream market share, cheap Asian imports through FTA routes, and substitute materials** (advanced plastics, composites, advanced steel, titanium) in aerospace and medical applications [F] (AR2026 p.76, p.78). Note the direction: the competitive pressure the company identifies is on **downstream value-added products**, which is exactly the part of the chain NALCO has just exited by winding up UADNL [AI].

blocks.text: NALCO competes on cost, not on customers, and its cost position rests on three things, of which none is a commercial achievement. **First, geology and a lease**: captive bauxite at Panchpatmali with royalty of roughly Rs 400-450 per tonne, against Chinese refiners running on imported Guinea bauxite whose cost structure management describes as "pretty high" [MC] (CALL May 2026; CALL Nov 2025). **Second, captive coal-fired power**: 96-97% self-generated at Rs 3.15 per unit, 31% of the cost of a tonne of metal [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). **Third, an import-parity umbrella on domestic metal**: management confirmed that customs duty plus inland transport puts domestic realisation roughly 10% above LME, and explicitly declined to say whether that premium would be maintained - "That we cannot disclose it now. That is our pricing policy" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

**All three legs are conferred, and two are policy-dependent.** The bauxite lease is granted by the state and South Block expires 19.07.2029 with an unknown renewal premium. The coal advantage has already narrowed to Rs 200-300 per tonne against linkage coal after the GST compensation cess was withdrawn. The ~10% domestic premium depends on the import duty structure, which is a Finance Act decision, not a NALCO decision. **A cost moat that is granted can be re-priced by the grantor** - which is a different risk profile from a moat that was built [AI]. What NALCO does own outright is the integration itself: the physical adjacency of mine, refinery, smelter, coal block and port, which no competitor can replicate with capital alone and which is the honest core of the investment case [AI].

subsections.title: The two questions the scores cannot answer

items: **Where exactly is NALCO on the global alumina cost curve, and at what alumina price does the refinery stop making money?** The claim to be "Lowest-Cost Producer of Bauxite & Alumina in the World" is attributed to a Wood Mackenzie report that is not in the evidence [MC] (PPT Sep 2026; SCREENER). Management's Rs 20,000-22,000 per tonne alumina cost implies roughly $230-253 per tonne at about Rs 87/$ [E], which would leave a margin at the guided $300-310 - but that cost figure is an unaudited call statement and excludes nothing explicitly, not even depreciation and royalty allocation. **Until the cost curve position is independently evidenced, the depth of the moat is an assertion** [AI].

**Will the bauxite leases be renewed, and at what royalty premium?** South Block expires 19.07.2029 - inside a five-year DCF horizon. Management believes the Mineral Conservation rules provide a 20-year renewal to a government company but said the premium "is not known to us till now. That depends upon the government policy", and separately noted that post-2015 iron ore renewals carried 150% additional royalty [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). **The one factor scoring 8 has an expiry date and an unpriced renewal cost** [AI].

blocks.text: **The moat is real, structural and irreplicable - and it is a cost moat that does nothing for price.** FY26 is the proof. NALCO ran every asset above nameplate, set records in bauxite, hydrate, calcined alumina, cast metal, power and coal, improved caustic consumption by 20%, eliminated grid power purchases and cut employee cost - and revenue still grew only 6.3% and EBITDA margin still fell, because the alumina price dropped 37% [F] (AR2026 p.43, p.79-80); [F] (NUMBERS). **A moat that cannot prevent that is a moat on the cost line only.** Its economic value is that NALCO survives cycles that kill marginal producers - which is genuinely worth something, and is visible in a Rs 8,408 cr cash pile built through a 37% alumina price collapse - but it is not a moat that converts industry growth into shareholder returns [AI].

subsections.title: Why TAM cannot be translated into company revenue

blocks.text: **Illustrative share arithmetic, labelled as such and used only to demonstrate the gap** [E]: NALCO's FY26 metal volume of 4,74,319 MT is 0.63% of the 75.3 Mn MT projected global market and 7.7% of India's 6.122 Mn MT total consumption. If Indian consumption grew at the top of the stated 7.8% range for five years it would reach roughly 8.9 Mn MT [E]. **NALCO's metal volume in that year would still be about 4.7 lakh tonnes**, because the smelter is physically capped at 4.60 lakh TPA nameplate and the 0.5 MTPA expansion does not commission until December 2030 or early 2031 on management's own timetable [MC] (CALL May 2026). Its implied share would fall from 7.7% to about 5.3% [E].

**This is the single most important structural fact in the report: for the entire five-year DCF horizon, Indian aluminium demand growth cannot raise NALCO's metal volume by one tonne.** It can only raise the price. Any argument that connects India's import gap to NALCO's revenue is, for five years, a price argument wearing a volume argument's clothes [AI].

blocks.text: **The honest bottom-up statement is therefore: NALCO's revenue over the next five years is a fixed metal volume times a variable metal price, plus a rising alumina volume times a falling alumina price.** Management's own FY27 arithmetic makes the trade explicit - a $400 per tonne higher metal price would give "comfort" against an alumina price decline worth "maybe around Rs.1,000 crores or Rs.1,200 crores" of adverse impact [MC] (CALL May 2026) [AI].

items: **Concentration on the supply side is extreme and Chinese.** China accounts for 59.35% of world production and its 45 Mn TPA ceiling against 46 Mn TPA of need makes it a net importer - which is structurally supportive of the metal price [F] (AR2026 p.75, p.77). Alumina supply concentration is shifting to Indonesia, where new refineries have run ahead of new smelters, creating the surplus that is compressing NALCO's alumina realisation [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026).

**NALCO's alumina channel is a monthly tender.** About four shipments of 30,000 tonnes a month, typically three spot and one term at 11-12% of LME; no long-term contracts currently in place, though Middle East parties have approached for one-to-three-year terms [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). **There is no distributor, agent or offtake network disclosed.**

**NALCO's metal channel is domestic and price-listed.** 4,61,081 t of 4,74,319 t sold domestically in FY26; pricing is a published formula revised every three days; premium set by six-monthly export tender; the Board approved new policies during FY26 for sale of alumina to micro and small enterprises and for bulk alumina sales in the domestic market [F] (AR2026 p.44, p.13); [MC] (CALL Feb 2026).

**Customer concentration, as disclosed:** no single customer exceeded 10% of total revenue in FY26 (one reached 12.41% in FY25); four customers (three in FY25) each exceeded 10% of the Chemical segment, together accounting for Rs 2,483.89 cr against Rs 3,317.65 cr for three customers in FY25 [F] (AR2026 p.255). **Read both ways**: on a total-revenue basis concentration improved; within the alumina segment, four customers on Rs 4,885 cr of segment revenue is roughly half the segment in four hands, and none of them is named [AI].

**Geographic channel risk is concentrated and unquantified.** Management has said 40-50% of alumina exports historically went to the Middle East, that this has been disrupted by war and by the Strait of Hormuz route closing, forcing road routing, and that the outlook "will depend on the war when the war ends. It's very difficult to predict" [MC] (CALL May 2026). **No country-level export disclosure exists to size this** [F] (AR2026 p.255 gives only India versus outside India) [AI].

subsections.title: Themes present in the narrative but not supported by the evidence

items: **Defence and aerospace aluminium.** The vehicle for this - the 50:50 UADNL joint venture with MIDHANI for a 60,000 TPA high-end alloy plant at a Rs 4,542 cr project cost - was found commercially unviable, the Ministry of Mines directed winding up, and the Board consented on 10.04.2026. Management's reason was unambiguous: transportation demand had not grown, "defence sector requirement was very less", and "even the IRR with the capex investment was coming negative" [F] (AR2026 p.90, p.228); [MC] (CALL May 2026). **The theme is not merely unproven; it has been formally abandoned** [AI].

**Critical minerals and lithium.** KABIL was incorporated in August 2019. Seven years later NALCO has invested Rs 40 cr, five Argentine lithium properties have completed non-invasive exploration, invasive Phase 2 began January 2026, and commercial viability will be assessable only "next one and a half years" [F] (AR2026 p.90, p.228); [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Feb 2026). The proposed restructuring would raise NALCO's stake from 40% to 60% of a pre-revenue venture with authorised capital doubling to Rs 1,000 cr [F] (AR2026 p.228). **Real optionality, zero revenue, and NALCO's exposure is increasing** [AI].

**Rare earths and gallium from red mud.** Three separate pilot-scale arrangements: NML Jamshedpur (methodology development, "one and a half to two years to set up this whole technology"), a Chennai party with a reactor at the mines whose results "have not come till now", and BARC for gallium from Bayer liquor. Management: "presently, these all are at pilot scale level... It will take another two, three years to firmly decide upon the value" [MC] (CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). Rs 2.51 cr sits in intangible assets under development for a fly-ash alumina recovery pilot [F] (AR2026 p.82). **Nothing is capitalised, nothing is quantified, nothing is in revenue** [AI].

**Green or low-carbon aluminium premium.** 198.40 MW of wind (307 MU) and 1,060 kWp of rooftop solar sit against a 1,200 MW coal-fired captive plant generating 6,953 MU - renewables are about 4% of generation [E] (AR2026 p.43, p.47; PPT Sep 2026). No green premium realisation is disclosed anywhere. The annual report itself states that "the lack of carbon pricing/green procurement policy leaves green investments unrecovered" and identifies EU CBAM and India's CCTS as cost threats requiring substantial investment [F] (AR2026 p.76). **The company is describing decarbonisation as a cost, not a revenue opportunity, and a reader should follow its lead** [AI].

**Value-added products as a margin lever.** Rolled products run at about 2,000 tonnes a month against a target of 2,500, and a 60,000 t alloy-grade wire rod mill is roughly two years away - together a low single-digit percentage of 4.7 lakh t of metal [MC] (CALL May 2026). The ingot-to-wire-rod premium actually **fell** from about $10,000 to $6,000-7,000 on the commentary given in February 2026 [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). **Mix improvement is not currently paying** [AI].

**Maharatna upgrade.** Mentioned once, inside a director's biography, as something the company is being prepared for [F] (AR2026 p.37). No application, timetable or criteria are disclosed. **Aspiration, not a theme** [AI].

**Long-term alumina offtake contracts.** Management repeatedly describes trying to sign one-to-three-year contracts and long-term relationships with global smelters [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Feb 2026; CALL May 2026). As of the May 2026 call: "Now at present, we don't have long term because since the pricing is very low, we are not going for the long term now" [MC] (CALL May 2026). **Intention, not contract** [AI].

blocks.text: **Two themes survive the evidence test - integration and the Indian supply deficit - and both have a catch.** Integration is already fully reflected in a 44% operating margin and a 40% ROCE; it is the reason the company earns what it earns today, not a source of future improvement. The Indian deficit is real and large, but NALCO's metal volume is capped until roughly FY31, so for the entire forecast horizon the deficit reaches the company only through the LME price, which the deficit does not set - China does [AI]. Of the seven themes a reader is likely to encounter in narrative about this company, one has been formally cancelled (defence alloys), three are pilot-stage after five to seven years (lithium, rare earths, gallium), one is described by the company itself as an unrecovered cost (green), one is not paying (value-added mix), and one is an aspiration in a biography (Maharatna). **The structural case for NALCO is the integration and the cash - not the optionality** [AI].

blocks.text: The forecast in this report is not ours to invent. It is the base-case projection carried in our valuation data, and we interpret it rather than replace it.
